At the time of collection. The dissenting view is that of the Tashbetz in a responsum, and his words require careful qualification. If there is such tumult from war or plague, may Hashem protect us, that no market price or ordinary buying and selling exists and every person is occupied with escaping for his life, it is obvious that property should not be sold then. Such a sale would resemble a sale without proper announcement, or a sale made at night or when workers do not ordinarily enter and leave. Indeed, Yirmiyahu was astonished when, with the Babylonian siege works already approaching the city, Hashem commanded him to buy a field. The Taz writes similarly. But this is not the case established by the Tashbetz's proof from the Mishnah about waiting to bring a cow to the market. His proof must concern a time when society continues to function and sales still occur, but property prices are severely depressed. He infers from Rashi that where one can wait for the animal to be brought to a major market, one does so, and from this he extends waiting to depressed land values. That inference is difficult. In the relation between debtor and creditor, the beginning of Bava Kamma says that if the creditor accepts payment according to his present legal entitlement he takes it now, and if he insists on other property he must take it at the future higher value. This implies that a creditor who takes the property he is legally entitled to need not wait until summer merely because everyone knows the field will then be worth more. The Baal HaTerumot, shaar 3, cites the Ramban that the same Gemara proves one need not wait for a later rise in value. Perhaps the Tashbetz distinguishes between a living debtor and orphans, following Tosafot in Eruvin who connect the rules of announcement with the rule of waiting for the marketplace. The Rambam requires a longer announcement process for orphans than for a living debtor, suggesting additional protection for heirs. Even so, the proof is not decisive. If the creditor himself says, "Do not sell now, because the low price will leave my debt unpaid; I am willing to wait," no one prevents him from waiting, especially when that also benefits the debtor. The dispute arises when the creditor demands payment now and refuses to wait for prices to rise. The Mishnah concerning consecrated property is different because there the consecrated estate itself is the claimant whose value we seek to maximize. Waiting for the market directly benefits the party entitled to the proceeds. That does not show that an ordinary creditor can be forced to postpone payment solely for the debtor's benefit. Nor is there a clear basis to distinguish orphans from a living debtor on this point without evidence. Tosafot's question from the sixty day announcement for consecrated land does not prove otherwise. Even if the announcement period is longer there to increase the return, it does not follow that every case must be delayed until the season of maximum value. The fixed announcement process can be required without indefinite market timing. Still, there is some support for the Tashbetz's distinction between a living debtor and heirs. Bava Kamma 7b asks that forcing a creditor to take property at a future high valuation would lock the door before borrowers, and the Gemara ultimately finds a possible application in a woman's ketubah, whose ordinary collection is from inferior land. Why not establish the case with adult heirs, from whom ordinary creditors also collect inferior land and where the concern of locking the door is weaker because lenders do not ordinarily anticipate the borrower's death? This may indicate that in the case of heirs the Sages indeed require waiting for a more favorable market, so the Gemara could not use heirs for the immediate choice between taking now and accepting the future high valuation. Rashi's language also supports this. He explains the ketubah case by saying that the husband gave her a divorce in Tishrei rather than simply saying that he died in Tishrei, suggesting that the rule would differ with heirs. Likewise, in Eruvin Rashi mentions estate property in connection with waiting to bring assets to a better market. The Derishah's attempt to limit that passage to a voluntary sale by an administrator is strained. The Talmud also says generally that consecrated property does not wait to bring an animal to market, whereas with orphan assets we do wait when the market day or market place is near. This suggests a real distinction between heirs and other sellers. Although the Rambam's reading of that Mishnah may differ, his commentary to the Mishnah indicates that one does not seek profit in consecrated property, which itself suggests that ordinary private property can sometimes be delayed for a better market. The Beit Yosef cites the Rashba against delaying a sale, but the Rashba's proof concerns a living debtor. In my view there is therefore room to distinguish heirs. The Beit Yosef may also have objected only where the delay itself creates a concrete risk of greater deterioration, as during war when land may soon become abandoned or damaged. In such a case land resembles movables, for which the Sages avoid delay because of the risk of loss. If no such risk is present, waiting for heirs may be appropriate when a substantially better market is near. The matter therefore depends on beit din's assessment. If the expected delay protects the estate without materially endangering the creditor or the property, the Tashbetz's ruling has substantial support. If delay creates a realistic danger of further loss, beit din may shorten even the announcement process, just as it does with perishable movables. Everything follows the circumstances seen by the judges.
But if they did not examine the appraisal carefully. See Sema, seif katan 11. We are dealing with the view of the Maggid Mishneh, whose explanation is that they did not carefully examine the appraisal and did not write an iggeret bikoret, meaning that this occurred at a time or in a place where announcement is not required. The Kesef Mishneh had difficulty with his explanation, for this is precisely the concluding clause, "and likewise if they sold land at a time," etc. Is it the Rambam's manner to repeat the same matter twice without any purpose? It appears that an iggeret bikoret is certainly the document of announcement that they give to a creditor when land has been appraised to him, so that he may consume the produce once the days of announcement have been completed. But what connection does a purchaser of the field have to the announcement? He merely has a deed of sale from beit din that he purchased the field, and from the time he gives the money he consumes the produce like any other purchaser. Accordingly, the Rambam is dealing with two forms: where the property was appraised to the creditor, and where it was sold to another. In both, if they erred by one sixth, the sale stands, but not if they erred by more. Both cases are necessary. One might have thought that a purchaser who acquired from beit din has the law of other purchasers, for whom there is no law of ona'ah with respect to land, whereas a creditor did not purchase the property, but it was merely conclusively assigned to him by appraisal, and there one can distinguish between one sixth and more than one sixth. Conversely, one can also say that with respect to a creditor, since his lien rests on the field and, in any event, an appraisal can be reversed, they are not so exacting, and therefore both cases are necessary. This is the Rambam's intent when he says, "but if they did not examine the appraisal and did not write an iggeret bikoret," which, as stated, refers to the creditor himself, to whom an iggeret bikoret is relevant; "and likewise if they sold," etc., which refers to an ordinary purchaser. Regarding both he says that the law depends on whether the error was one sixth, and the same law applies to both. It is true that in the first clause he should not have written "their sale stands" or "is void," but rather "their appraisal stands" or "is void." He was simply drawn after the terminology of the purchaser, although in truth the transfer to the creditor can also be considered a sale. This may be said according to the Maggid Mishneh. The Rambam in this clause adopted the language of the opening clause of the Mishnah, "the appraisal of the judges," etc. The Ramban, according to the Rambam's view, establishes it as a case where they appraised the property to the creditor himself, as cited in the Ran. The Beit Yosef, however, explains that these are two separate clauses. The first clause deals with a place and time where announcement is required, but they did not carry it out with the requisite care, while the second deals with a place where announcement is not required. In truth, the Rambam's wording points in that direction. The Shach, however, already wondered about this. The Gemara asks from the Mishnah, which states that if they erred by one sixth their sale is void. Either way there is a difficulty: if they made an announcement, then even if property worth two hundred was sold for one hundred their sale stands; and if they did not make an announcement, they erred in an explicit Mishnah and the transaction must be reversed. The Gemara answers that the case is a place where announcement is not required. Why did it not answer simply that they did make an announcement but did not perform it with proper care, as the Kesef Mishneh explains the Rambam? At first glance this requires study. It appears, however, that independently of this there is a difficulty in understanding what is meant by careful appraisal and announcement. If they appraised according to law through three judges, that itself is a proper appraisal. What additional exactitude is relevant? And if they did not act according to the law and established procedure of appraisal and announcement, the entire proceeding was erroneous and should be reversed. Why should the superior power of beit din make an error up to one sixth stand? It therefore appears that where the property is of a type, or the matter occurs at a time or place, for which announcement is not required, even if they nevertheless announced it, according to the Rambam their power is not thereby enhanced. The reason is that since there is no obligation upon them to announce, the matter is not incumbent upon them and they do not appraise and scrutinize as carefully, as the Sema writes in seif katan 16. This is straightforward. Accordingly, if they erred in the law and thought that a matter which truly requires announcement does not require it, yet as an added precaution and to strengthen the transaction they nevertheless announced it, then even in such a case, according to their understanding the duty was not incumbent upon them, and they did not examine and scrutinize it as carefully as required. What difference is there, from their perspective, whether in truth announcement was required or not? On this basis, the Rambam states two clauses. The first is where announcement was in truth required, but they erred and thought it was not required; therefore they did not examine and scrutinize properly, because we say that it was a matter they did not regard as incumbent upon them. Nevertheless, since they did announce it, their power is enhanced so that an error up to one sixth stands. The second is where the matter truly does not require announcement. The Rambam thereby teaches two substantial points: one case where they erred and thought announcement unnecessary, and one where announcement was in truth unnecessary. In the latter he teaches that an error of more than one sixth voids the transaction. One might have thought that since announcement is truly unnecessary, their power should be even stronger. He therefore teaches that even so, their sale stands only up to one sixth. This is precise. The Shach's difficulty is now resolved. Until the Gemara answered the foregoing question by establishing the Mishnah in a place where announcement is not required, and the initial assumption had been that announcement is required in every case, the Kesef Mishneh's answer, that they did not scrutinize properly, could not be given, because of the difficulty stated above: what additional scrutiny is relevant? Once the Gemara teaches that there are places and times where announcement is not required, however, the matter can properly be explained as above, that they erred and thought announcement unnecessary. The matter is therefore well resolved.
And if beit din wished, etc. According to the view of the Rosh in Perek Almanah and the view of the Tur, the explanation is that the purchaser deceived the orphans and their land was sold too cheaply. The choice is therefore in the hands of the orphans: either to void the sale, or to say, "Return to us the amount by which you deceived us." It cannot mean that the orphans deceived the purchaser, because the Rambam's view, as explained in seif 5, is that in such a case there is no recovery at all. Yet one must understand the Rambam's reason, "the power of an ordinary person should not be more stringent than theirs." What greater stringency is present here? Either way the purchaser can argue: if you come against me with the law of an ordinary private transaction, there is no ona'ah with respect to land; and if you come with the special power of the orphans, the sale is void. What basis is there for requiring return of the amount of ona'ah while maintaining the sale? It must be that the Rambam holds that the Sages equated movables and land in every respect concerning an appraisal by beit din, so that no distinction should be made among appraisals. With movables, certainly, if the orphans wish the purchaser to return the amount of ona'ah and maintain the sale, the sale stands and he returns the ona'ah, for their power should not be inferior to that of an ordinary person, regarding whom the law is that the purchaser acquires and returns the ona'ah. Therefore the same is true of land, since the Sages made no distinction among appraisals. The Rambam gave this reason with respect to movables, and the same law follows automatically for land. The Rambam inferred this from the Mishnah, which groups them together under "the appraisal of the judges." This includes movables as well, as the Gemara says regarding matters for which no announcement is made, meaning movables. Since the Mishnah grouped them together, it follows that one law applies to them. However, from the words of the Ran and other authorities it appears that the orphans were not the ones deceived. Rather, the purchaser was deceived, meaning not an ordinary purchaser but the creditor to whom the land was appraised in satisfaction of his debt. In that case, even though the law is that an error of one sixth voids the transaction, since the property was appraised to him against his will, as the Ramban writes, nevertheless, if the orphans wish to maintain the transaction and return the ona'ah to him, they may do so. This rule applies to movables and certainly to land. According to this, where the property is land and the orphans were deceived, perhaps they cannot compel the purchaser to maintain the sale and return the ona'ah, because he can argue whichever law favors him. The Rambam would then agree with the Rosh in this case. Why should we create a new dispute without necessity? For this reason, here in this siman, where the Mechaber copied the Rambam's wording exactly and without alteration, he did not bring the dissenting view of the Rosh. If the Rambam is explained according to the second interpretation, the Rosh does not disagree. In Even HaEzer siman 104, however, where the Mechaber explicitly wrote a case in which the orphans were deceived, he brought "there are those who disagree," meaning the Rosh, who indeed disputes that ruling. See there. It appears that according to the Rambam, if the orphans were deceived by more than one sixth but nevertheless wish to maintain the sale, the sale stands. This follows from the Rambam's ruling below in the laws of ona'ah that even where the error is sufficient to void the sale, the party who caused the deception cannot retract. The power of an ordinary person should not be greater than that of the orphans. Yet perhaps, according to the Sema's reason below that the deceiving party cannot retract because a sinner should not profit from his wrongdoing, that rationale does not apply here, since the transaction was carried out by beit din. This remains strained and requires study.
And regarding movables, the Gemara states that the reason is lest they be stolen. There is room to question the law where the movables are in the creditor's possession because he seized them as collateral. Perhaps in such a case the concern underlying the omission of announcement no longer applies, for the concern that they may be stolen is absent. The creditor is a paid bailee, either because of the benefit described by Rabbi Yosef or because he is holding them against money owed to him. What concern of theft is there, and unavoidable accidents are uncommon? From Tosafot, who ask that the movables of orphans are not subject to the creditor's lien and answer that he seized them against the money owed, it appears that they nevertheless hold that there remains a concern of an unavoidable accident, or that the Sages made no distinction, or that they were also concerned for a loss to the creditor.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
נעשה כמי שטעו בדבר משנה אפילו לא טעו כלל בשומא מ"מ כיון שלא היה כפי תקנת חז"ל:
דאין לב"ד למכור וכו' עיין תומים דמיירי דיש מנהג סוחרים נוהגים למכור וליקח רק זילא נכסי בזו דעת המחברים הללו דמוכרין אבל אם אין שער מקח וממכר כלל לגודל הרעש לכ"ע אין מוכרין דהוי כאלו לא הכריזו או כאלו נמכר בשעה שאין הפועלים נכנסים כלל. ועיין תומים דהבאתי כמעט ראיה ברורה לדברי רשב"ץ החולק וס"ל בשל יתומים אין מוכרין וממתינים עד שעת היוקר והרשב"א בעל דיעה קמייתא מיירי בלוה עצמו שבאים להתפרע מנכסיו בזו לא החמירו להמתין ע"ש. ולכך כתבתי דאפילו לדעת רבינו ב"י החולק ארשב"ץ וס"ל דאף בשל יתומים אין ממתיני' היינו ביש חשש לפנינו דח"ו אם ימתין עד יעבור רעש יתקלקלו הקרקע ביותר מכמה טעמים אבל אם אין חשש זה מצוי לפנינו אף להב"י אין ראיה דאין להמתין עוד כתבתי לדעת הב"י בכה"ג דאין ממתיני' אם נראה לב"ד למעט בהכרזה כדי למכור טרם יבאו ימי הרעה ח"ו אף זה רשות בידם:
אחריות על יתומים היינו מה שירשו מאביהם אבל אין חל על נכסים שלא ירשו וקמ"ל דה"א מאן דזבין בב"ד קלא אית ליה ובטוח שלא יבא ערעור וכלוקח שלא באחריות דמי קמ"ל דמ"מ אמרינן ט"ס הוא ואחריות על יתומים גמרא:
שוה ק' בק"ק עיין מש"ל ס"ס ס"ו דאיכא למ"ד דוקא בכה"ג ולא יותר ע"ש:
אבל אם לא בדקו וכו' עיין תומים דדעת המ"מ דהכל מיירי במקום שא"צ הכרזה ודלא יקשה א"כ סיפא דקתני וכן אם מכרו קרקע הא היינו הך צ"ל דרישא מיירי שהחליטו למלוה בשומתו וטעו וסיפא איירי דבהכרזה לקחו אחר על פי השומא וקמ"ל במלוה וקמ"ל בלוקח וצריך לומר מכרן דקתני ברישא לשון מושאל וכוונתו שומתן. אמנם הכ"מ יצא לדון ולומר דמיירי דבעי הכרזה ומ"מ אם לא דקדקו בו כראוי דינו בשתות ולא יותר. ובזה איירי הך בבא דלא דקדקו כראוי. ובסיפא במקום שא"צ הכרזה. ועיין תומים דכתבתי פי' לדבריו מהו שלא דקדקו היינו דחשבו שהוא מדבר דא"צ הכרזה רק ליפוי כח עשו הכרזה ולכך אינו מועיל רק עד שתות דלדעתם א"צ הכרזה ולא דקדקו כראוי:
פחות משתות מכרן קיים דבזה למדו קרקע מן מטלטלין דכמו במטלטלין בפחות משתות הוי מחילה ולית ביה קפידא כן עשהו בזה בקרקע אבל בשתות כיון דבמטלטלין ליכא מחילה לא השוו מקרקע למטלטלין דשם קנה ומחזיר אונאה משא"כ בזה כיון דקפידא הוא הכל בטל:
או במקום שנהגו וכו' כי מלעיגים על אותם בני עיר שהם כל נכסים הנקנים באכרזתא כי רובם ב"ח וקרקעות שלהם נמכרים ולכך נמנעו לקנות דבר באכרזתא ומטעם זה בטלו שם אכרזתא גמרא:
מכרן בטל הטעם הואיל ואינם מחוייבים בהכרזה לא רמיא עלייהו דב"ד לדקדק בהכרזה ולכך לא אלים כחו:
דכיון שהכריזו וכו' דאדרבא כיון דאין על ב"ד חיוב להכריז והם מ"מ הכריזו ש"מ דדייקי יותר בהכרזה ויותר אלים כח ב"ד:
ויחזירו אונאה וכו' עיין תומים דהרא"ש מפרש דמיירי דהפחת הוא ליתומים וס"ל להרמב"ם דיכולים לתבוע שיחזיר להם האונאה ויתקיים המקח ובזה חולק וע"ש מ"ש דס"ל לרמב"ם דלא חילקו חכמים בין שומת מטלטלין לשומת קרקע אבל אני כתבתי די"ל דיתומים אינו ללוקח ויש להם רשות להחזיר האונאה ולקיים המקח ולא קשה הא לדעת רמב"ם אם נתאנה לוקח לעולם לא מצי לחזור דכאן מיירי במלוה שנשום ליה בע"כ. ודינו בשתות וס"ל אם ירצו יתומים להחזיר לו אונאה מקחו קיים ולפ"ז י"ל בדין הרא"ש הרמב"ם מודה להרא"ש דאין רשות ביד יתומים לומר החזר לי אונאה וקיים המקח. גם אם היה פחת ליתומים יותר מכדי שתות אם יכולים יתומים לומר אעפ"כ נקיים המקח כדלקמן בהל' אונאה ע"ש בתומים דהדבר צ"ע:
העבדים וכו' שמא יברחו ומטלטלין ושטרות שמא כשיתאספו רבי' להכרזה עי"כ יגנבו אותן ומיירי לדינא דגמרא שכתב מא"ק או שתפסינהו מחיים דאל"כ למה נמכור הא לא משתעבדי ועיין תומים ואע"ג דמלוה התופס הוי ש"ש מ"מ אף לפסידה דמלוה חששו חז"ל:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
It is treated like an error in an explicit Mishnah. This is so even if there was no error in the valuation itself, because the procedure did not follow the enactment of the Sages.
For beit din should not sell, etc. See Tumim. This refers to a market in which merchants are still buying and selling, but property prices have temporarily fallen. These authorities hold that the property may be sold. If, however, due to great upheaval there is no functioning market at all, everyone agrees that it should not be sold. That is equivalent to selling without proper public announcement, or at a time when buyers do not come to market at all. In Tumim I brought nearly conclusive proof for Rashbatz, who disagrees and holds that property of orphans should not be sold at a depressed price, but should wait for a better market. Rashba, who gives the first view, may be speaking of the debtor himself, whose property is being collected, where the Sages did not require waiting. Therefore, even according to Beit Yosef, who disagrees with Rashbatz and holds that orphan property need not wait, this may apply only where there is a present concern that waiting until the turmoil passes could cause the land to deteriorate further for various reasons. Where no such concern exists, there is no clear proof that Beit Yosef would refuse to wait. I also wrote that according to Beit Yosef, in a case where waiting is inappropriate, beit din may shorten the announcement period if necessary to sell before the anticipated bad conditions arrive.
Liability rests upon the heirs. This means upon property they inherited from their father, not their independent property. The novelty is that one might have thought that a purchaser from beit din assumes the sale is secure and therefore resembles one who purchased without warranty. The ruling teaches that omission of warranty is treated as a scribal error, and the heirs' inherited estate remains responsible. This is from the Gemara.
Worth one hundred for two hundred. See what I wrote at the end of siman 66, that some authorities limit the rule specifically to this degree and not beyond it.
But if they did not examine properly, etc. See Tumim. Maggid Mishneh understands the entire discussion to concern a place where no announcement is required. Otherwise the concluding clause, 'likewise, if they sold land,' would simply repeat the same law. According to him, the first clause concerns beit din assigning the property directly to the creditor by appraisal and erring, while the second concerns a purchaser who bought following announcement based on the appraisal. The word 'sold' in the first clause is therefore borrowed language meaning appraisal. Kesef Mishneh instead understands the first clause to concern a place where announcement is required, but beit din failed to conduct it with proper precision. Their error is then governed by the one sixth rule. The concluding clause concerns a place where no announcement is required. In Tumim I explained that 'they did not examine properly' means that they mistakenly believed the property was of a type not requiring announcement, although they nevertheless announced it merely to strengthen the sale. Since in their view announcement was unnecessary, they did not perform it carefully enough, and the sale is protected only within one sixth.
If the error was less than one sixth, the sale stands. Here the Sages analogized land to movable property. Just as an error of less than one sixth in movable property is waived and does not indicate significant objection, so too here. But at exactly one sixth, since movable property law no longer treats the error as waived, they did not fully equate land to movable property. With ordinary movable property the sale stands and the overcharge is returned; here, because the error shows substantial objection, the entire judicial sale is void.
Or in a place where the custom is, etc. In such places people mock those who purchase property at judicial auction because most such property belonged to debtors whose land was being forcibly sold. Buyers therefore avoid judicial auctions, and for that reason the Sages dispensed with announcement there. This is from the Gemara.
The sale is void. Since beit din was not obligated to announce, it was not especially charged with meticulous announcement, and therefore the judicial sale does not receive enhanced protection.
Since they announced, etc. The opposite reasoning is that precisely because announcement was not required, yet beit din nevertheless undertook it, this shows that it exercised extra care, and its act should therefore receive greater force.
And they return the overcharge, etc. See Tumim. Rosh explains that the estate was underpaid, and understands Rambam to hold that the heirs may demand return of the overcharge while keeping the sale in force. Rosh disagrees. I wrote there that Rambam may hold that the Sages did not distinguish between appraisals of movable property and land. I also suggested that the heirs themselves are not the purchaser and may therefore return the overcharge and preserve the sale. This does not conflict with Rambam's ordinary rule that a purchaser who was underpaid cannot rescind, because here the case may involve a creditor who received land by appraisal against his will. If so, Rambam may agree with Rosh that heirs cannot insist, 'Return the overcharge and keep the sale,' where the estate itself was underpaid. Whether heirs may choose to preserve a sale even where the error exceeded one sixth is also discussed in Tumim and requires study.
Slaves, etc. There is concern that slaves may flee. With movable property and promissory notes, gathering a crowd for announcement may facilitate theft. This refers to the Talmudic rule where movable property was expressly encumbered with land or seized during the debtor's lifetime. Otherwise such property would not be subject to collection at all. See Tumim. Although a creditor who seizes is a paid custodian, the Sages were concerned even for loss to the creditor.

mechaber.he: אפוטרופוס או ב"ד שלוו לצורך היתומים מוכרים שלא בהכרזה ופורעים וכן ב"ד דזבין ואחריותא איתמי אם טרפו ממנו גובה הלוקח שלא בהכרזה:
mechaber.en: A guardian or a lawyer for the purposes of known orphans not in the declaration and riots, and in the Dassbin and the responsibility of the Ithmimi if he was stripped of the high helm which did not declare:

baer_hetev.he: ופורעים. זהו כדין דסעיף הקודם. היכא דזבני למזוני ולכרגא ומטעם שכתבתי שם עכ"ל הסמ"ע ולא דק דכאן הטעם הוא דהוי כבעל דבר שרוצ' לפרוע בעצמו ובאמת שאם אינם רוצים לפרוע מדעתם זה תלוי בפלוגתא שבסי' קכ"ג ס"א ע"ש. ש"ך:
baer_hetev.en: and broken. This is the previous section. It is a sign that I have written there, and not a minute, the taste is deo as a person who is running away from himself and the truth that if they don’t want to get rid of their own science, it depends on the patriarchy. “Third:

beer_hagolah.he:
הרא"ש והר"ן בפרק אלמנה ניזונית בשם הרמב"ן מחס"א
שם מחס"ב
beer_hagolah.en:
The Rosh and Ran in Almanah Nizonet, in the name of Ramban, from section 1.
There, from section 2.

beur_hagra.he: אפוטרופוס או כו' וכן ב"ד כו'. כן הוכיחו תוס' שם פ"ז א' ובגטין נ"ב מדפריך בערכין כ"ב א' תנן שום היתומין כו' ולא משני בכה"ג:
beur_hagra.en: A guardian or a priest, and also in the “D. Yes, the name of Dr. A. and Gen. Gen. Gen. Genuine has been shown to be “infected” and “nothing of the genitals” rather than the other two in the league:

chelkat_mechokek.he: במתנה בשעת מותו. לאו דוקא בשעת מותו רק החילוק הוא בין מתנה למכר והטעם הוא כי הצמידים מחוברים במלבוש רק שיש להם שם בפני עצמו וכל שיש לו שם בפני עצמו אעפ"י שמחובר לקרקע אינו מכור ובמתנה קנה הכל ע"כ הנותן מתנה לאשה כל מלבושיה סתם אף הצמידים המחוברים בכלל וליכא למימר למה לא פירשה האשה שיכתוב לה אף הצמידים משום שהיא מתביישת לשאול ממנו אבל בשעת נשואין כל מה שכותב לה אז הוי כמכר שהיא מוכרת עצמה לו ואינה מתביישת לו' תכתוב לי הצמידים בפני עצמם ומאחר שלא כתב לה הצמידים בפני עצמם ויש להם שם בפני עצמם אינם בכלל המלבושים והצמידי' הם שלו:
chelkat_mechokek.en:
at the time of his death. At the time of his death, only the burden is between a gift to the mine and the taste is that the bracelets are connected in the dress only that they have a name in itself, and that he has a name in his face, and that he is connected to the ground is not an addict and the gift of the woman is not allowed to ask for anything that she is sold to ask for
Shame on him will tell me the bracelets themselves and because he has not written the bracelets before themselves, and they have no name for themselves at all, the clothes and the bracelets are his:

meirat_einayim.he: מוכרי' שלא בהכרזה זהו כדין הנ"ל בסעיף דלפני זה היכא דזבנו למזוני ולכרגא ומטעם שכתבתי שם:
meirat_einayim.en: They sell without announcement. This follows the law in the preceding seif concerning a sale for food or governmental taxes, for the reason I wrote there.

siftei_kohen.he: מוכרין שלא בהכרזה. זהו כדין הנ"ל בסעיף דלפני זה היכא דזבני למזונות ולכרגא ומטעם שכתבתי שם עכ"ל סמ"ע ולא דק דכאן הוא הטעם דהוי כבעל דבר שרוצה לפרוע בעצמו ובאמת שאם אינם רוצים להפרע מדעתו זה תלוי בפלוגתא שבסי' ק"ג ס"א ע"ש וק"ל וע' בב"י:
siftei_kohen.en: They sell without public announcement. The Sema writes that this is governed by the preceding seif, where they sell for maintenance and the head tax, for the reason he explained there. This is imprecise. Here the reason is that the estate stands in the place of a litigant who wishes to pay the debt himself. In truth, if the creditors do not wish to accept payment voluntarily from the estate, the matter depends upon the dispute in siman 103, seif 1. See there, and see the Beit Yosef.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: או ב"ד שלוו וכו' הטעם כדי שיהיה שכיחי אנשים המלוים אותו ואם נעשה תמיד שומא והכרזה ימנעו אנשים להלוות:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: Either in his or so on the taste to be common to people who speak him and if we always do so, the declaration will prevent people from borrowing:

mechaber.he: הא דאמרינן שאם טעו ב"ד ופחתו שתות או הותירו שתות מכרן בטל היינו כשהורידו לבעל חוב בשומת ב"ד אבל ב"ד שמכרו קרקע או עבדי' של יתומים שוה מנה במאתים אין הלוקח יכול לחזור בהם לא יהיה כח הדיוט חמור מכח היתומים וכן הדין באפוטרופוס שמכר קרקע ועבדי' שאין הלוקח יכול לחזור בהונייה כדין הדיוט (וי"א דכל שפחתו או הותירו שתות מכרן בטל (טור בשם ה"ר יונה והרא"ש):
mechaber.en: The rule that a sale is void when beit din erred upward or downward by one-sixth applies when they transferred property to a creditor at beit din's appraised value. But if beit din sold land or slaves belonging to orphans that were worth one hundred for two hundred, the purchaser cannot retract. An ordinary person's power should not be stronger than that of the orphans. The same rule applies when a guardian sold land or slaves: the purchaser cannot retract because of the price discrepancy, just as in an ordinary sale. {Rama: Some say that whenever the price was lower or higher by one-sixth, the sale is void.}

baer_hetev.he:
שמכרו. ר"ל אפי' כדי לפרוע לב"ח ודלא כנרא' מלשון הב"ח דאף היכא דמכרו לצורך פרעון בע"ח גם כן דינו כאילו הורידו לבע"ח ע"ש דליתא וע' בהה"מ פי"ג מהלכות מכיר' דין י"א. שם:
בהונייה. ע"ל סי' רכ"ז סל"ד:
baer_hetev.en:
That they sold. Meaning even if the heirs sold the property in order to pay a creditor. This is unlike what might be inferred from the Bach, namely that where they sold specifically in order to pay a creditor the law is as though they had directly placed the creditor into possession. That is not so. See Maggid Mishneh, chapter 13 of Hilchot Mechirah, halachah 11. Shach.
With its overcharge. See siman 227, seif 34.

beer_hagolah.he: כן כ' הרמב"ם שם בפי"ג מה' מכירה שנ"ל כן והביאו הטור סי"ב וכ"כ ה"ה שם בשם הרמב"ן ושכן עיקר
beer_hagolah.en: Rambam writes so there in chapter 13 of Hilkhot Mekhirah, stating that this appears correct to him. Tur cites him in seif 12. Maggid Mishneh likewise writes there in the name of Ramban and states that this is the principal ruling.

beur_hagra.he:
הא דאמרי' כו' לא יהיה כו'. כמ"ש בגטין נ"ב א' משוך פירי מיתמי כו' לא יהא כו':
וי"א דכל כו'. לא קאי אלא אב"ד אבל אפוטרופוס דינו כשליח ודינו יתבאר בס"ו וכן בטור והר' יונה כ' דב"ד כו' וכן מסתבר לא"א כו' וכן לקמן סי' רכ"ז ס"ל כ' בהדיא דדין אפוטרופוס כדין שליח ועמ"ש בס"ו:
beur_hagra.en:
The rule that, etc.; the strength should not be, etc. This is parallel to Gittin 52a, where the Gemara states that the power of the beit din should not be less than that of ordinary persons.
Some say that every, etc. This applies only to the beit din. A guardian has the law of an agent, as Tur, Rabbenu Yonah, and the later ruling in siman 227 make clear. See citation 227.

meirat_einayim.he:
הא דאמרי' שאם טעו ב"ד ופחתו כו'. כשהורידו לב"ח ואע"פ דהמשנה הנ"ל דשום הדיינים והרמב"ם והמחבר לעיל בס"ג כותבין כולם ל' מכירה צ"ל דגם זה מכירה קרי ליה מה שהב"ח מקבל אחר השומא והכרזה אבל הרא"ש ואינך גאונים פירשו המשנה דשום הדיינים הנ"ל דקתני פחתו או הותירו שתות מכרן בטל כו' כפשוטו דאיירי גם במכרן ללוקח ומטעם שאכתוב בסמוך:
בשומת ב"ד אבל ב"ד שמכרו כו'. הטעם דדוקא כשנותנין להמלוה בחובו דאז צריך לקבלו כמו ששמוה שאין נותנין לו בפחות מכדי שיעור ששמוהו מ"ה בין פחתו שתות או הותירו שתות המקח בטל אבל כשהב"ד מוכרין השדה לאינש דעלמא דאינו צריך ללקחו בשומת ב"ד אלא ברצונו תלוי לקיחתו מהן כמו שאר הדיוטים שמוכרין זה לזה קי"ל כר"מ דאין אונאה לקרקעות והיינו דוקא אם טעה הלוקח וקנהו ביוקר בכפל אבל אם טעו ב"ד ומכרו בזול מכרן בטל בשתות וכ"כ הרמב"ם בהדיא שם בפי"ג דמכירה והראב"ד והרא"ש ס"ל דגם בטע' הלוקח ביתר משתות המכר בטל כיון דקנ' בשומת ב"ד ולא עלה על דעתו שיאונה הלכך בכה"ג אפי' בקרקעו' קפדי אינשי וזהו טעם י"א שכ' מור"ם אזה:
meirat_einayim.en:
What we say, that if beit din erred and undervalued, etc. This concerns a case where beit din placed property in the hands of a creditor. Although the Mishnah, Rambam, and Mechaber use the language of a sale in the law of judicial appraisal, delivery to the creditor after appraisal and announcement is also called a sale. The Rosh and other Geonim, however, understand the Mishnah literally as also covering a sale to an outside purchaser.
In a judicial appraisal, but if beit din sold, etc. The reason is that when beit din gives land to the creditor for his debt, he must accept it at their appraised value, so if they erred by one sixth in either direction the transaction is void. But when beit din sells the land to an outsider, he is not obligated to purchase at their valuation; his purchase is voluntary like an ordinary private sale, and we rule that land has no ona'ah. Thus if the purchaser overpaid, even substantially, the sale may stand. But if beit din erred by selling too cheaply, their sale is void at a one-sixth error. Rambam states this explicitly in chapter 13 of Hilchot Mechirah. Raavad and Rosh hold that where the purchaser erred by more than one sixth the sale is also void, because he relied on beit din's valuation and did not anticipate being overcharged. This is the basis of Rama's dissenting view.

[" כדין הדיוט כו'. ע' לקמן סי' רכ\"ז סעיף ל\"ד ודו\"ק:"]
siftei_kohen.en:
This refers to where they placed the creditor in possession. This is the principal explanation. The words, 'But if the beit din sold,' mean even where they sold in order to pay a creditor. This is contrary to what appears from the Bach, who holds that even a sale made to satisfy a creditor has the same status as placing the creditor directly in possession. That is incorrect. According to this, the Bach's question upon the Tur, who cites Rabbenu Yonah as disagreeing with the Rambam, is also resolved. The Rosh writes in Rabbenu Yonah's name that the purchaser relies upon the beit din, meaning even where the sale was made to pay a creditor. Examine this carefully. See also the Maggid Mishneh, chapter 13 of the Laws of Sale, law 11, where the Mechaber's understanding of the Rambam is explicit, contrary to the Bach.

The same law applies to a guardian. Not completely. With beit din, an error below one sixth leaves the sale intact. By contrast, with beit din there is no distinction, because just as the orphans rely on the judges, the purchaser relies on them not to act unjustly or show improper favoritism. Beit din thus serves both sides. See siman 227 for a dissenting view based on Rashi, who explains that where beit din's sale is invalid for the orphans it is also invalid for the purchaser. On either rationale, the preceding case can result in cancellation.
And specifically... The Gemara says that just as a widow acts alone, so an ordinary agent acting alone is distinguished from beit din. Here, however, a single judge acting under royal authority functions as a court-appointed judicial officer, and his act is legally equivalent to that of the authority that empowered him. See Bava Kamma 113b. The same applies to his appraisal error.

מכרו ע"י שליח. אף דע"כ הי' צריך שומת ג' בקיאים דאפי' אלמנה שמכרה בלא שומא המקח בטל להרב' פוסקים ועוד דהוי טעות כד"מ שמכרו בלא הכרז' וע"ב בשומא מיירי ואפ"ה מכרו בטל דהקנין צריך שיגמר ע"פ ב"ד ולא ע"י שלוחם ואף דודאי אם בעה"ב אומר לשליח מכור בכמה שישומו שלשה או שאומר לו בכמה למכור ונתאנ' דינו בבעה"ב שנתאנ' ולא בשליח שנתאנ' דהא הוא נתאנה בעצמו והשליח לא נתאנ' כלל ולא יכול לומר לו לתקוני שדרתיך ולא לעוותי דהשליח לא עיוות כלל וא"כ ה"נ דמי להא ודוחק לומר דמיירי ששלחו שליח למוכרו במקום אחר שלא במקום השומא וכעין שכתבתי לעיל דכל כה"ג הו"ל לפוסקים לפרושי הכא טעמא אחרינא איכא דדוקא כשהמעש' הקנין נתקיים מיד ב"ד מעשיהן קיימי' ולא כשנעש' הקנין ע"י שליח שלהם:
שופט הממונה. נראה דוקא בישראל שהי' חייב לעכו"ם שנתחייב לו בדינא דמלכותא ולכן מכירתו מכיר' כדינא דמלכותא אי נמי בגוונא שכתב הריב"ש שם כאלמנה שמכרה כיון דהדין הוא דאלמנ' מוכרה שלא בב"ד וכשמכר' בדיני עכו"ם לא הוי גזל אבל ישראל שחייב לחבירו והולך המלו' בדיני עכו"ם ומכר קרקע של לוה שלא ברשות ב"ד דהוי כגזלן כיון שעשה שלא ברשות ב"ד המקח בטל דהוי כהכיר בה שאינו שלו ולקחו:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en:
They sold through an agent. The property necessarily had to be appraised by three experts, for even a widow who sells without appraisal has, according to many authorities, made a void sale. Moreover, it would otherwise be an obvious error similar to beit din selling without public announcement. The case must therefore involve proper appraisal, and nevertheless the sale is void. The reason is that the acquisition must be consummated directly by beit din, not through their agent. Certainly, if an owner tells an agent, Sell at whatever price three experts appraise, or tells him a specific price at which to sell, and an overcharge occurs, the law is that the owner himself was overcharged, not the agent. The owner cannot tell the agent, I sent you to improve matters, not to harm them, because the agent did not deviate at all. Our case would therefore seem comparable. It is strained to say that the authorities discuss only a case in which beit din sent the agent to sell in another place, not the place of appraisal, and the authorities should have specified such a circumstance. Rather, there is another reason: only where the act of acquisition itself is directly effected by beit din do their acts have special validity. When the acquisition is effected through their agent, it does not.
An appointed judge. It appears that this applies specifically where a Jew owed a non-Jew and became obligated to him under the law of the kingdom, so the judge's sale is valid under dina d'malchuta. Alternatively, it applies in the type of case described by Rivash, such as a widow who sold property, because the law permits a widow to sell without beit din, and therefore a sale conducted through non-Jewish courts is not theft. But if one Jew owes another and the creditor goes to a non-Jewish court, which sells the borrower's land without permission of beit din, the creditor is like a robber because he acted without beit din authorization, and the sale is void. It is like a purchaser who knew the seller did not own the property.
